In [[mathematics]], '''Böhmer integrals''' are [[integral]]s introduced by Paul Böhmer generalizing [[Fresnel integral]]s.{{sfnp|Böhmer|1939}}

The integrals are defined for all <math>x\geq 0</math> and <math>\alpha < 1</math> as{{sfnp|Oldham|Myland|Spanier|2008|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=UrSnNeJW10YC&pg=PA401 401]}} 
:<math>\operatorname{S}(x,\alpha) = \int_x^\infty t^{\alpha-1} \sin(t) \, dt, \quad \operatorname{C}(x,\alpha) = \int_x^\infty t^{\alpha-1} \cos(t) \, dt.</math>

When <math>\alpha=1/2</math>, Böhmer integrals reduce to Fresnel integrals <math>S(x), C(x)</math> by
:<math>\begin{align}
\operatorname{S}(x) &= \frac1{2}-\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\cdot\operatorname{S}\left(\frac1{2},x^2\right), \\[1ex]
\operatorname{C}(x) &= \frac1{2}-\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\cdot\operatorname{C}\left(\frac1{2},x^2\right).
\end{align}</math>

The [[sine integral]] and [[cosine integral]] can also be expressed in terms of the Böhmer integrals by{{sfnp|Oldham|Myland|Spanier|2008|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=UrSnNeJW10YC&pg=PA401 401]}}
:<math>\operatorname{Si}(x) = \frac{\pi}{2} -\operatorname{S}(x,0), \quad \operatorname{Ci}(x) = - \operatorname{C}(x,0).</math>
